newsitem.title: CENTRAL AFRICAN REPUBLIC: Fresh army revolt in Bangui, French troops patrol.
newsitem.headline: Fresh army revolt in Bangui, French troops patrol.

text.p: Dissidents in the Central African Republic's army mutinied for a third time this year on Saturday and French troops patrolled the streets of the capital to protect strategic points, military sources and witnesses said.

President Ange-Felix Patasse, speaking in Rome where he is attending the World Food Summit, played down talk of a revolt. "It is not a mutiny. Some common law prisoners have escaped and are trying to create panic. That is all," he said.
But Prime Minister Jean-Paul Ngoumpande, in a broadcast address to the nation, urged all sides to hold their fire and to return their weapons to their respective armouries.
"Nothing would be more serious for the country than a new bloody episode among its children," he said.

Troops from former colonial power France, who put down a revolt that threatened to topple Patasse in May, patrolled the deserted city centre with presidential guard loyalists. "French soldiers have been deployed in Bangui to assure the safety of certain sensitive areas," a French official said in Paris.
France has an important military base in Central African Republic, one of the world's poorest countries, under a defence accord. Patasse, a civilian, invoked the accord in May to secure French help.
Bangui could play a key role in France's contribution to a multinational force to help protect and feed refugees in Zaire.
Scattered firing could be heard early in the day.

Markets remained closed throughout the city but there were no immediate reports of looting that accompanied the May mutiny and a pay revolt in April. Hospital sources said two people had been admitted with gunshot wounds.

Witnesses said dissidents had seized the general secretary of Patasse's ruling Movement for the Liberation of the Central African People (MLPC), Joseph Vermond Tchendo, and the head of the police national force, Ernest Latakpi.

The revolt began at Kassai Barracks on the eastern fringe of the capital, about three km (two miles) from the city centre. "They broke into the armoury around midnight and stole arms and then firing broke out," a senior loyalist officer said.
Witnesses and military sources said the dissidents ventured out early on Saturday but later returned to Kassai barracks.
A soldier contacted by telephone by Reuters in the barracks said earlier about 200 soldiers had gone to various districts to try to disarm militia loyal to Patasse.
The whereabouts of Tchendo and Latakpi were not clear.
Army sources linked the latest revolt to a bid late on Friday to arrest a nephew of former military leader Andre Kolingba, whom Patasse defeated in a 1993 presidential poll.
The nephew, an army captain, was out on parole after serving a jail sentence for embezzlement and other charges, they added.

Sources close to the dissidents said they had revived demands for wages from 1992 and 1993 and for Patasse to revoke a decree ordering the Regiment for the Operational Defence of the Territory (RDOT) to Bouar, 80 km (50 miles) from Bangui. The regiment was heaviliy involved in the earlier revolts.
A national conference after the May revolt agreed on a number of reforms to improve the lot of soldiers by creating a professional army with a fuller role in the life of the nation.

But friction remains. The army is dominated by members of former self-styled emperor Jean-Bedel Bokassa's Gbaka tribe but Kolingba's Yakoma tribe is well-represented. Bokassa, ousted in 1979 and later disgraced, died on November 3 aged 75.
